questions.question: Which broad area takes the largest share of UK public spending?

options.B: Social protection, such as pensions and benefits

questions.why: Social protection, led by the State Pension, is the largest spending function in HM Treasury PESA data.

questions.question: Which area is usually the second-largest part of UK public spending after social protection?
questions.why: PESA consistently shows health as the second-largest function after social protection.

questions.question: A chart shows public spending in cash terms rising every year. What can you safely conclude?

options.B: Cash figures include inflation, so you must check after-inflation figures to know if real spending rose
options.C: Spending as a share of GDP rose

questions.why: Cash figures are not adjusted for inflation, so a cash rise can be flat or falling in real terms.

questions.question: Which three taxes raise the most money for the UK government?

options.A: Income tax, National Insurance and VAT
options.B: Council tax, fuel duty and stamp duty
options.C: Inheritance tax, capital gains tax and alcohol duty
options.D: Corporation tax, tobacco duty and air passenger duty

questions.why: HMRC and OBR receipts data show income tax, NICs and VAT as the three largest sources.

questions.question: Which single tax raises the most money?
questions.why: Income tax is the largest single source of UK government receipts.

questions.question: When public spending is higher than taxes and other receipts, how is the gap mainly covered?
questions.why: The gap is public sector net borrowing, which is not a tax or receipt.

questions.question: Which of these is a tax on spending rather than on income?
questions.why: VAT is charged on goods and services people buy, so it is a tax on spending; the others are charged on income or gains.

questions.question: If a chart says income tax provides about a quarter of government receipts, what does that mean?

options.B: It is income tax's share of total revenue, not anyone's tax rate
options.C: Households pay a quarter of their income in tax
options.D: The basic rate of income tax is 25%

questions.why: A share of total revenue describes where the money comes from, not the rate any person pays.

questions.question: Which household income group pays the largest share of all income tax?
questions.why: ONS and HMRC data show the highest-income fifth pays most income tax in total.

questions.question: Roughly what share of all income tax do the top 1% of income taxpayers pay, according to HMRC?
questions.why: HMRC estimates have put the top 1% share at well over 25% of income tax for many years.

questions.question: As a share of disposable income, indirect taxes such as VAT take more from which households?

options.C: Both take exactly the same share

questions.why: ONS Effects of Taxes and Benefits shows indirect taxes are a larger share of disposable income for the poorest fifth.

questions.question: Which of these are counted as direct taxes on households in ONS figures?

options.A: Income tax, National Insurance and council tax

questions.why: ONS classes income tax, employee NICs and council tax as direct taxes.

questions.question: A page says households in a group pay, on average, 35% of gross income in all taxes. What does this mean?

options.A: Each person faces a 35% income tax rate
options.B: Direct plus indirect taxes average 35% of that group's gross income; it is not a personal tax rate
options.C: That group pays 35% of all tax revenue

questions.why: A household average combining direct and indirect taxes is neither a personal rate nor a share of total revenue.

questions.question: As household income rises, what generally happens to direct taxes as a share of gross income?

options.C: The share stays exactly the same

questions.why: ONS data show direct taxes take a rising share of gross income as income rises.

questions.question: A page shows a 'typical family' paying a stated amount of tax, labelled as an illustration. What is it?

options.B: A worked example built from assumptions, not a measurement of real households
options.C: An official record of a real family
options.D: The UK median household's tax bill

questions.why: An illustration shows how rules apply to assumed circumstances and is not a measured statistic.

questions.question: In which broad type of industry do most people in the UK work?
questions.why: ONS workforce jobs data show over four in five jobs are in services.

questions.question: Employment rose in the year after a new government policy. What does this alone show?

options.B: Employment changed, but the figures alone do not show what caused it

questions.why: A change following an event does not prove cause, as many other factors affect employment.

questions.question: Average pay rose 20% in cash terms while prices rose 25%. What happened to pay after inflation?
questions.why: When prices rise faster than cash pay, real pay falls.

questions.question: A pay chart is labelled 'real terms'. What does that mean?

options.A: Pay is adjusted for inflation so different years can be compared fairly
options.B: Pay is shown exactly as it was paid at the time
options.C: Pay is shown after income tax only
options.D: Pay is shown only for full-time workers

questions.why: Real-terms figures remove the effect of price rises so pay in different years can be compared at the same price level.

questions.question: What is the most common housing tenure in England?

options.A: Owning a home, outright or with a mortgage

questions.why: The English Housing Survey shows owner-occupation is the largest tenure, about two-thirds of households.

questions.question: Which country do UK residents visit most often on trips abroad?
questions.why: ONS Travel Trends consistently show Spain as the most visited country by UK residents.

questions.question: A holiday chart shows no figure for a year because the survey was paused. How should you read that gap?

options.B: As a year with no measurement, not zero, and not to be joined across
options.C: As the average of the years either side
options.D: As the same as the year before

questions.why: A missing year means no data was collected, so it must not be read as zero or silently filled.

questions.question: In England, infant classes (ages 5 to 7) with one teacher are legally limited to how many pupils?
questions.why: The School Admissions (Infant Class Sizes) regulations cap infant classes in England at 30 per teacher.

questions.question: A chart shows average class size for primary schools in England. Can you directly compare it with Scottish secondary schools?

options.A: Yes, all UK class sizes are the same measure
options.B: No, it is a different nation and school phase, measured separately
options.D: No, because Scotland has no schools data

questions.why: Class size statistics are collected separately by each nation and differ by school phase, so comparisons need care.
